messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is an eighteen-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a junior tax consultant at a small accounting firm in Atlanta. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure he made to his employee assistance program counselor approximately three weeks ago.

Approximately four months before seeking help, Kofi attended a gathering at the apartment of a colleague he had met shortly after starting his job. He did not know the other people present well. At some point during the evening he was separated from the small group, led into a back room by a man he had trusted enough to follow, and raped. He remembers the sound of the front door slamming shut somewhere in the apartment as it happened — a sound that seemed to seal off any possibility of help arriving. The man had raised his voice at one point, a sharp, commanding shout, and Kofi had gone still. He remembers a specific taste, something metallic and sour, that he cannot fully account for and cannot fully forget.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi told no one. He returned to work, filed spreadsheets, answered emails, and sat in meetings. On the surface very little changed. Beneath it, almost everything did. The memories that returned to him were not narrative — they arrived as images, vivid and fragmentary, a hand, a wall, a shadow across a ceiling. At other times there was no image at all, only an abrupt wave of the same terror and shame he had felt that night, arriving without warning and without context, as though his body had retained the emotional record even when his mind refused to supply the scene. Most disorienting of all, the taste returned. Sitting at his desk eating lunch, or drinking coffee in the break room, that same metallic sourness would appear on his tongue and he would have to set down whatever he was holding and wait for it to pass.

Kofi began to reorganize his life around what he could not yet name. He stopped going anywhere he did not already know well. He had come to believe that in an unfamiliar environment he would have no way of reading the exits, the people, the likelihood of danger, and that belief felt less like anxiety and more like clear-eyed reasoning. When strangers approached him — on the street, in a parking garage, even in the lobby of his own office building — he felt a threat that seemed to him entirely proportionate. He was certain that his body was simply registering information that other people chose to ignore. He stopped taking the elevator when male colleagues were already inside it. He began arriving to the office before anyone else and leaving after most people had gone, a habit that his supervisor initially praised as dedication before noticing that Kofi flinched visibly when a door opened behind him, and that he had begun declining all client-facing assignments that required visiting unfamiliar offices.

That flinch had become a source of private humiliation. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a well-meaning colleague sent him halfway out of his chair. He began sitting with his back to the wall in the conference room, positioning himself so that no one could approach him from behind. What frightened him most was not that these responses were happening, but that he could not make them stop. He had always thought of himself as composed and capable, someone who had worked hard and arrived early at a professional life most people his age had not yet reached. The gap between that self-image and the person who could not ride an elevator with a man he had known for months felt unbridgeable.

What finally brought him to speak was a performance review. His supervisor noted, gently but in writing, that Kofi had become withdrawn and was limiting his own opportunities. Reading those words, Kofi understood that the life he had been quietly protecting was already contracting around him. He came to his first session hoping, above everything else, to feel safe enough to go back to being who he was before — and terrified, in equal measure, that the person he was before no longer existed.
